The expression "a bridge too far" originated with British General Frederick "Boy" Browning, who said "I think we might be going a bridge too far" to General Roy Urquhart before Operation Market Garden began in September 1944 [d8]. This was confirmed by General Urquhart himself in his 1958 memoir Arnhem, where he ascribed the phrase to Browning [d2]. The phrase was then recorded by author Cornelius Ryan in 1973 while researching his 1974 book about Operation Market Garden, after which it took on a life of its own as an idiom [d8][d1]. One source (Quora) incorrectly attributes the phrase to Field Marshal Montgomery as a retrospective comment [d5], but this is contradicted by the more credible and detailed accounts in d2 and d8, which clearly place the remark with Browning before the battle. The idiom has since come to mean an overly ambitious goal or act of overreaching, inspired by the ultimately failed Allied operation to capture key bridges in the Netherlands [d7][d6].
